item.title: Artspace Guåhan to open ‘You Are Here’ exhibition
item.description: Artspace Guåhasn will open its new exhibition, You Are Here, on Oct. 15, at its studio in Tamuning. The exhibition brings together different artistic perspectives and explores how personal histories, identities, experiences, and surroundings can influence how people understand themselves and the world around them.
item.content:encoded:
Artspace Guåhasn will open its new exhibition, You Are Here, on Oct. 15, at its studio in Tamuning.

The exhibition brings together different artistic perspectives and explores how personal histories, identities, experiences, and surroundings can influence how people understand themselves and the world around them.

The exhibition centers on the question, “What does HERE mean to YOU?” and invites visitors to consider their own connections to place and belonging through the artwork on display.

Artspace Guåhan will bring together artists with different perspectives and ask visitors to consider what being “ here ” means to them. Deane Jessee-Jones, secretary of the board of directors, says the exhibition supports local artists of varying ages.

She said, “We do not collect any commission… all of the profits go directly to the artist.”

Artspace Guåhan is a Guam-based nonprofit that works to make art accessible and provide opportunities for local artists to exhibit and connect with the community.

The opening runs from 6 to 7:30 p.m. and will include an opportunity to meet the artists.

The exhibition will remain on display through Dec. 3.

You Are Here is free and open to the public.

item.title: U.S. Supreme Court hears arguments in Andersen open detonation case
item.description: The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday, Washington, D.C. time, in a case involving an open detonation pit on Andersen Air Force Base. The group Prutehi Guåhan sued the Air Force in 2022, arguing that open detonation of hazardous waste and unexploded ordnance endangers Guam’s environment, cultural heritage and ancestral lands.
item.content:encoded:
The U.S. Supreme Court heard arguments on Wednesday, Washington, D.C. time, in a case involving an open detonation pit on Andersen Air Force Base.

The group Prutehi Guåhan sued the Air Force in 2022, arguing that open detonation of hazardous waste and unexploded ordnance endangers Guam’s environment, cultural heritage and ancestral lands.

In May 2021, the Air Force applied for a three-year renewal of its hazardous waste facility permit with the Guam Environmental Protection Agency. In court filings, Prutehi Guåhan stated that the Air Force failed to conduct an environmental assessment of its actions as required by the National Environmental Policy Act.

The case was dismissed in the District Court of Guam, but the 9 th Circuit Court of Appeals sided with Prutehi Guåhan and reinstated the case.

The Supreme Court is considering whether the Air Force’s request to renew its permit would be a “final agency action” that can be reviewed by the courts. Justices are also considering whether federal agencies must comply with NEPA requirements before seeking to renew environmental permits.

During oral arguments before the court, Department of Justice attorney Sopan Joshi argued that filing a permit application is not a final agency action.

“It’s a request to someone else to take action,” he said. “Filing a permit application triggers a back-and-forth process whose outcome is, by definition, a moving target until a decision on the permit is issued. Treating an application as final would just lead to a multiplicity of suits throughout a permitting process, which I think defeats the whole point of the finality requirement.”

Chief Justice John Roberts, a George W. Bush appointee, asked Joshi when the Air Force’s decision to operate the detonation pit would be considered final.

“So are you saying that there’s no point at which the Air Force’s decision can be challenged?” he asked. “The Air Force’s action is never final and, therefore, never reviewable?”

“The application is never going to become final agency action,” Joshi said. “And there is no cause of action under NEPA itself. Congress didn't provide one. So any review would have to go through the [Administrative Procedure Act], and I don't think the APA provides a cause of action for this application at any point in time.”

Earthjustice attorney Caroline Flynn, representing Prutehi Guåhan, said the Air Force’s final action is clear.

“We know that the Air Force is settled on that decision because it has, in fact, been acting on them past -- you know, by continuing these detonation operations past September 2021, when they otherwise would have ceased.”

The justices will consider the arguments, and a ruling will likely take several months.

item.title: ‘Struggling to keep this government going’: Apatang warns of furloughs, rising austerity after signing strained CNMI budget
item.description: The CNMI is facing deep fiscal strain as Gov. David M. Apatang defended his line‑item vetoes in the newly signed fiscal 2027 budget, which is built on $100.7 million in projected General Fund revenues. Apatang signed the budget Tuesday night, ending a five‑day partial shutdown that left non‑essential employees without pay.
item.content:encoded:
The CNMI is facing deep fiscal strain as Gov. David M. Apatang defended his line‑item vetoes in the newly signed fiscal 2027 budget, which is built on $100.7 million in projected General Fund revenues.

Apatang signed the budget Tuesday night, ending a five‑day partial shutdown that left non‑essential employees without pay.

Apatang said he vetoed several provisions he deemed unconstitutional or financially impossible, including a mandate requiring the administration to “front‑load” $16 million to the Public School System. He said the CNMI cannot afford the upfront payment and must instead fund PSS monthly. The Senate’s final budget version allocates $25 million for PSS—down from the $32 million proposed by both the governor and the House.

“It breaks my heart to reduce PSS funding,” Apatang said, adding that a three‑day school week would be unacceptable but may be unavoidable unless the PSS board finds operational efficiencies.

The governor said the administration is “scraping the bottom of the barrel,” warning that furloughs—estimated at up to 400 employees—may be necessary once Civil Service Commission regulations are finalized. He also confirmed retirees will lose their 25% government contribution after Oct. 15, though he is searching for funds to soften the impact.

Apatang defended his administration against criticism over the CNMI’s fiscal collapse, saying he inherited years of unresolved audit findings and depleted federal relief funds.

“I didn’t spend all this money,” he said. “We’re struggling to keep this government going.”

He urged agencies to tighten operations, reduce expenses, and avoid unnecessary vehicle use. He also asked Commonwealth Public Utilities Corp. to reconsider CUC’s proposed rate increase, calling it “a drastic burden” residents cannot afford.

On tourism and economic recovery, Apatang said federal immigration and travel policies continue to hinder the CNMI’s ability to rebuild air service and visitor arrivals. He said he has repeatedly asked federal officials to visit the Commonwealth and understand its strategic importance.

With three months left in his term, Apatang said the next administration will face a difficult road.

“Good luck,” he said. “I’ll pray for you. It’s going to be a tough one.”

item.title: The U.S. last held a public execution in the 1930s. The Pentagon wants to change that
item.description: The Pentagon says it will livestream the planned military execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009. Hasan, 56, has been on military death row since his conviction and sentencing in 2013. His case returned to the public spotlight this week when the Pentagon announced that President Trump had approved his death by firing
item.content:encoded:
The Pentagon says it will livestream the planned military execution of Nidal Hasan, the former Army psychiatrist who killed 13 people and wounded 32 at Fort Hood, Texas, in 2009.

Hasan, 56, has been on military death row since his conviction and sentencing in 2013. His case returned to the public spotlight this week when the Pentagon announced that President Trump had approved his death by firing squad — a first for the military since World War II .

The Pentagon says Hasan's execution will take place on the afternoon of Dec. 3 at Fort Hood, the site of his shooting rampage. On Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said the proceedings would be available for public viewing.

"We'll make sure that people are able to watch it, that it's public, because people need to understand that there's serious consequences for these types of things," Hegseth said in a video interview with Real America's Voice, a right-wing streaming network.

The Pentagon confirmed to NPR in a statement Friday that the execution "will be livestreamed," saying details would follow.

But much remains uncertain. Legal experts have said Hasan could delay his execution by years if he decides to file a habeas corpus appeal in federal court. Michael Radelet, a professor emeritus at the University of Colorado Boulder who studies capital punishment, says outside groups could potentially challenge the livestream plans too.

"Hegseth is a rather controversial person," Radelet told NPR. "If he says, 'Do it this way,' it's not at all clear that it will actually be done that way."

If it does come to pass, it would be the first public execution in the U.S. in nearly a century — and the first ever to be livestreamed.

"Public executions have typically been held in authoritarian countries to instill fear in the population and to show the power and control of the government," Robin Maher, the executive director of the nonprofit Death Penalty Information Center, told NPR. "We're not aware of any regulation or historical precedent for a [U.S.] military execution to be livestreamed on the internet or otherwise made widely available to the public."

The last high-profile public execution in the U.S. was the hanging of Rainey Bethea — a Black man convicted of raping a white woman — in 1936. The case drew national attention.

Roughly 20,000 people gathered in the western Kentucky city of Owensboro, where workers had built a gallows near the riverfront, according to NPR station WKMS . People celebrated with "necktie" parties the night before and sipped soft drinks at the scene in what attendees and historians describe as a festive atmosphere.

"They sold sandwiches and they sold Coca-Colas, and you'd have thought it was a big picnic or something," attendee Bill Shelton recalled in a 2013 oral history interview with the Daviess County Public Library.

The spectacle prompted a public backlash over the perceived barbarity of executions. Kentucky held a "semipublic" hanging in a prison yard the following year, Radelet said, before outlawing public executions altogether in 1938. There haven't been any in the U.S. since.

He said the closest example was the lethal injection of Oklahoma City bomber Timothy McVeigh in 2001. The Justice Department made a closed-circuit telecast available for designated survivors and victims' loved ones to watch remotely; 232 of them gathered in a viewing room in Oklahoma City to do so.

"It's like getting rid of the guillotine — when it's gone, it's gone," Radelet said. "There was no serious discussion about bringing it back."

He said public executions fell out of favor for two main reasons: They are no longer widely believed to be a crime deterrent, and authorities became worried that public executions — especially those that went wrong — would turn people against the death penalty.

In fact, as part of that shift, executions have become less visible over time, Maher said. Initially, she said, states would conduct them in the middle of the night. Now, she said, some states that still carry out the death penalty have limited access for media witnesses.

"We moved away from public executions quite deliberately because they had turned into spectacles. That was not sitting comfortably with people anymore," said Maher. "And I think there was a move away from that sort of circus environment to inside prisons in the middle of the night."

Tennessee's recent botched lethal injection of Christa Pike has reignited debate over the death penalty. Radelet thinks a firing squad execution — especially if it's livestreamed — could further diminish public support for capital punishment, already at a five-decade low .

"There probably wouldn't be too much blood, but enough to make people talk about it over their morning coffee, if they're not sick," Radelet said. "And that discussion might be yet another step towards abolishing the death penalty."

Justin Mazzola, deputy research director at Amnesty International USA, said in a statement that Hegseth's announcement "adds to the display of cruelty" seen recently with Pike's botched execution.

"The U.S. death penalty is irredeemably broken," he said. "It is high time that the U.S. authorities, at all levels, use their power to show human rights leadership and end this ultimate cruel, inhuman and degrading punishment once and for all."

Hegseth's comments were met immediately with questions, concerns and calls for reconsideration. On Friday, Vice President JD Vance told reporters , "if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."

Archbishop Paul S. Coakley, president of the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops, released a statement saying a public execution "will only further undermine the moral fabric of our nation and be a blight on the conscience of its people."

"In no way can Hassan's [sic] actions be condoned but this decision is a barbaric promotion of a culture of death and must be reconsidered," he wrote.

Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., wrote on X that he supports Hasan's death sentence, but called a livestream "beyond disgusting."

"Public executions are what oppressive dictatorships like Iran and Afghanistan do," he wrote. "It should not be happening in America."

Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., a member of the Senate Foreign Relations committee, similarly mused on CNN whether Hegseth is "mimicking ISIS executions." He called public executions "medieval" regardless of people's feelings about the death penalty itself.

The top Democrats on both the House and Senate Armed Services Committees issued statements condemning the Pentagon's plan. Jack Reed, D-.R.I., ranking member on the Senate Armed Services Committee, called it "another stunt by Secretary Hegseth to distract from his tenure's repeated failings" and "a gift to anti-American terrorist recruiters."

"The Trump Administration should reconsider this abhorrent move, which only gives the shooter what he wants: more attention and more control," Reed wrote.

item.title: U.S. working to reverse an Egyptian man's third-country deportation to Africa
item.description: The Trump administration on Friday said it has started to facilitate the return to the U.S. of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea, in a rare case of the government working to reverse a third-country deportation . A federal judge in Arizona earlier this week ordered the Department of Homeland Security to return Ahmed Soliman to the U.S. from the country in central Africa where he
item.content:encoded:
The Trump administration on Friday said it has started to facilitate the return to the U.S. of an Egyptian man who was deported to Equatorial Guinea, in a rare case of the government working to reverse a third-country deportation .

A federal judge in Arizona earlier this week ordered the Department of Homeland Security to return Ahmed Soliman to the U.S. from the country in central Africa where he has no ties, and respond how it plans to do so.

The administration said it is working "collaboratively" with Soliman's lawyers to find and contact him, and is "beginning the process to facilitate" his return, according to Friday's filings in the case from Timothy Courchaine, the U.S. Attorney for the District of Arizona.

Soliman, who is a gay, had been able to get an order from a U.S. immigration judge to prevent him from being deported to his home country, Egypt, where he could be persecuted for his sexuality.

Instead, the Trump administration deported him earlier this year to Equatorial Guinea, which ranks as one of the least free countries in the world, according to Freedom House , a nonprofit devoted to protecting and growing democracy, and human rights across the globe.

Arizona District Court Judge John Hinderaker, an appointee of President Trump, said that DHS violated the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment when it removed Soliman to a third country.

"It is unrebutted that he has since been held under armed guard; threatened at gunpoint; and arrested, beaten, and held incommunicado by Equatorial Guinean authorities," Hinderaker wrote in his Oct. 6 order.

The ruling comes even as the U.S. Supreme Court last week allowed the Trump administration to resume deportations of migrants to countries where they have no ties, at least for now, while agreeing to take the case up for full oral argument in December.

DHS told NPR in a statement this week that it would comply with lawful court orders and that Soliman would continue to receive due process.

"But the end result will be the same — he will not remain in the U.S. This administration will not ignore the rule of law," the DHS spokesperson added.

Dana Camilleri, one of Soliman's lawyers, said compliance means diplomats in Equatorial Guinea must work to facilitate Soliman's release. She is working to get a similar outcome for another client in the central African country, a gay Brazilian man.

" We're all just really hopeful that this could be the beginning of getting them home," Camilleri said. "Because they're in an awful situation, and our government put them there."

The office of the U.S. ambassador to Equatorial Guinea did not respond to a request for comment.

Soliman has been held under armed guard at a decommissioned hotel where he has been threatened at gunpoint, arrested, beaten and been unable to communicate with his family or lawyers, according to court filings .

Soliman emigrated to the U.S. from Egypt when he was a child, grew up in Arizona and became a green card holder. He lost his immigration status after a 2023 drug possession and aggravated assault led to a prison sentence.

That's when an immigration judge ruled he could not be sent to Egypt, where he would most likely be tortured.

The harm Soliman is alleged to have suffered in Equatorial Guinea could put the U.S. in violation of international law, according to Aaron Reichlin-Melnick, a senior fellow at the American Immigration Council. The council advocates for a fair process for immigrants in the U.S.

" We are signatories of the UN convention against torture, and domestic law makes it illegal to send someone to a place where they will be persecuted," Reichlin-Melnick said. " All of this really violates a lot of the basic principles of due process and human rights that Americans support," and serves as "a direct rebuke to the Trump administration's broader strategy of third country removals."

The Trump administration has made deals with over 30 countries to deport migrants to places where they have no ties or connections as part of the president's immigration crackdown.

Hinderaker's order to return Soliman marks the second time a judge has forced the government to return a third-country migrant from an African nation. A Colorado judge also ordered the return of Brayan Omar Sanchez Servellon , originally from Honduras, who was sent to the Central African Republic earlier this year.

item.title: Did Russia play by the rules in reporting lab worker's death?
item.description: A 28-year-old woman died in Russia last week and, since then, speculations about the case have ricocheted around the globe. The woman was a lab technician at a Russian research institute that studies the plague. As unverified rumors have circulated that she may have contracted the disease from a lab leak, President Trump, the World Health Organization and other leaders are asking for more informat
item.content:encoded:
A 28-year-old woman died in Russia last week and, since then, speculations about the case have ricocheted around the globe.

The woman was a lab technician at a Russian research institute that studies the plague. As unverified rumors have circulated that she may have contracted the disease from a lab leak, President Trump, the World Health Organization and other leaders are asking for more information.

Russia has insisted this is not a health emergency and stated that its health authorities have not found dangerous pathogens in any of the deceased woman's contacts.

But there are still far more questions than answers.

That uncertainty has global leaders and health experts turning to a law that obligates countries, including Russia, to share exactly this type of information. It's called the International Health Regulations or IHR.

On Wednesday, at a WHO press conference, Director General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus invoked IHR as the best way to determine current situation in Russia and determine the appropriate response.

"We don't yet have the full picture of this event," he said. "Timely, complete and transparent information sharing under the international regulations is essential to clarify conflicting reports and enable an accurate assessment of potential public health risks."

Here are the key things to know about the IHR and how it applies in today's world.

This law requires countries to share health information that could have international implications. It goes way back to the 1850s with cholera outbreaks in Europe, which led to the creation of guidelines for sharing disease information.

"That's very, very long for international law," says Alexandra Phelan , an associate professor at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health and senior scholar at the Johns Hopkins Center for Health Security. "Look at the negotiation documents and they're debating: Is cholera caused by a bacteria or miasma [a bad smell]? Like we're really right in the middle of germ theory."

Then, when WHO was founded in 1948, these regulations — then called the International Sanitary Regulations — were adopted. That was one of the organization's first moves. The law has since been amended and updated, most notably after the SARS or Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome outbreak in 2003 and most recently due to COVID-19 pandemic.

A country is supposed to notify WHO if the health event has the potential to cause an international health emergency.

Today, IHR is among the most widely ratified international treaties, with 197 signatories including the U.S. and Russia. (Even though the Trump administration says it has withdrawn from WHO, the U.S. is still bound by the IHR with the exception of some recent amendments.)

One of the core obligations in the law "is that parties or states must notify WHO within 24 hours of detecting a [serious health] event," explains Phelan.

Some events – like a case of smallpox or a new type of influenza — should immediately trigger a notification. For other situations, a checklist helps a country assess whether notification is needed.

Each year, she says, WHO receives thousands of notifications from all over the world and most turn out to be nothing.

Some people fear the Russian woman — who died Oct. 2 — had pneumonic plague. That's one of the diseases "explicitly listed" under IHR, says Phelan, as something to assess and notify the WHO.

However, Russia did not notify WHO about this woman's death. Instead, WHO learned about it through media reports and then, on Oct. 3, went to Russia seeking verification and additional information.

"Russia's response, firstly, was delayed," says Phelan. "But also it wasn't comprehensive."

It took Russia several days to respond. On Oct. 6, health officials told WHO there were no cases of plague in the region and that the woman was hospitalized with severe pneumonia of unknown origin before she died. They also explained that health authorities had placed about 200 contacts in quarantine.

WHO asked Russia for more information, including about lab tests conducted, public health measures and the health status of the woman's contacts. However, as with many international laws, there's no mechanism to make countries comply with the law and share information.

Phelan says the next few days and weeks will be key in understanding how much information Russia is going to share. If they aren't fully transparent, she hopes pressure from other countries either convinces Russia to comply with IHR or, at least, helps keep up the norm of other countries respecting IHR and notifying WHO about future health events.

That kind of notification is critical if the world is to be ready to respond and contain future outbreaks, says Lawrence Gostin , who directs the WHO Center on Global Health Law and is a professor at Georgetown University.

"This case shows the good, the bad and the ugly of the IHR," he says.

"Legally, this is the only thing that's holding Russia to account," Gostin explains. And yet, "you have countries that are hiding the ball."

He believes that the risk to the general population from the current situation in Russia is likely very low. But, for him, the fact that countries can disregard the IHR notification requirements is a "blaring siren about how unprepared we are" to quickly control health threats.

For stories about life in our changing world, subscribe to NPR's Global Health newsletter.

item.title: Five children are taken from their parents in 'Fjord,' which won top prize at Cannes
item.description: The gifted Romanian writer-director Cristian Mungiu makes tense realist thrillers that lay bare his country's history of corruption and authoritarianism. In Beyond the Hills , he took aim at intolerance within the Romanian Orthodox Church. In his 2007 masterpiece, 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days , he laid bare the cruelties of the communist dictatorship in the late 1980s. That film won the Palme d'Or
item.content:encoded:
The gifted Romanian writer-director Cristian Mungiu makes tense realist thrillers that lay bare his country's history of corruption and authoritarianism. In Beyond the Hills , he took aim at intolerance within the Romanian Orthodox Church. In his 2007 masterpiece, 4 Months, 3 Weeks and 2 Days , he laid bare the cruelties of the communist dictatorship in the late 1980s. That film won the Palme d'Or at Cannes and announced Mungiu as a major international talent.

A few months ago, Mungiu won a second Palme d'Or for his new drama, Fjord , which, in many ways, marks something of a departure. It's his first movie shot outside Romania, but even in a fresh setting, his eye for institutional oppression and hypocrisy is as sharp as ever.

Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve give superb performances as a married couple, Mihai and Lisbet Gheorghiu, who have just moved from Romania to a small town nestled among the fjords and mountains of Norway. They have five children; the oldest is in high school, the youngest still in diapers. They're also strictly observant Christians. In one scene, which features mostly English and some Romanian dialogue, they're singing hymns at home with some church friends when they get a visit from a friendly neighbor, Mia, and her teenage daughter, Noora.

The townspeople are welcoming at first, and Mungiu uses wide shots and long takes to immerse us in this open, bustling community. But things get unfriendly fast for the Gheorghius. One day, a school administrator notices that their eldest daughter, Elia, has bruises on her back, and overhears her and her brother talking about having been disciplined by their parents. A call is made to Child Protective Services, and with dizzying speed, the five Gheorghiu children — including the baby — are taken away from their parents and placed in foster care.

The rest of the film follows Mihai and Lisbet's efforts to get their kids back, pitting them against an unyielding Norwegian legal system. In the testimonies that emerge, we learn that one of their children had expressed anti-LGBTQ opinions in class. This raises the question of whether the Gheorghius were targeted for abusing their children, which they vehemently deny, or for refusing to adopt the progressive, secular-humanist values of their new home country.

For all the acclaim and awards it's received, Fjord has proven remarkably divisive for a Mungiu movie. Although the story was inspired by a widely publicized case from 2015 , involving a Romanian Norwegian family that endured a similar ordeal, some critics have accused the film of reducing the European welfare state to a straw-man villain — an overreaching government entity that denies parents due process. Others have claimed that such responses merely prove Mungiu's point about the intolerance of the left and how tribalism and racial and religious discrimination can arise even in ostensibly inclusive communities.

For my part, I found Fjord to be a blatantly yet skillfully manipulative drama that craftily withholds as much information as it reveals. Mungiu traffics in ambiguity, sometimes to the point of coyness. The episodes of alleged physical abuse are strategically obscured or kept off-screen. A plausible alternate explanation for Elia's bruises emerges, but it's never confirmed. Fascinatingly, the kids themselves never come right out and say whether they've been physically abused, and their silence on the matter feels dramatically evasive — but also, from a parent's perspective, eerily fitting. It's as if the film were saying that, with or without state interference, our children begin to become unknowable, drifting away from us, the moment they're born.

I thought a lot about my own kids while watching Fjord and the outrage I'd feel if they were taken away from me. I also sifted through my complicated feelings about my own distant evangelical-Christian upbringing. Stan and Reinsve's performances, full of tightly controlled sorrow and fury, make it easy to feel for Mihai and Lisbet, and to believe that they're genuinely good, loving parents, whether or not you share the rigidity of their beliefs.

And I suspect that, deep down, it's that rigidity that Mungiu takes the most issue with. It's no accident that the most sympathetic character here is that friendly neighbor, Mia, who turns out to be an attorney and agrees to represent the parents in court, noting, at one point, that she feels a moral obligation to defend the minority. Mia, for her part, isn't religious. Yet she's one of the few characters here who fully embraces the biblical commandment to love thy neighbor.
